title: Newton's Third Law
seo_title: Grade 8 Newton's Third Law Worksheets: Action-Reaction Forces and Collisions
standard_text: Apply Newton's Third Law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on Newton's third law (NGSS MS-PS2-1): action-reaction force pairs, collisions between objects of different mass, and designing bumpers, helmets and airbags. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
key_sub: Colliding objects push on each other with equal forces. The lighter object changes speed more.
body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. The two forces act on different objects at the same time, so they do not cancel.

In a collision, both objects feel forces of the same size. The object with less mass changes its speed more.

Engineers use this to design safer collisions: helmets, airbags, bumpers and crumple zones spread the force over a longer time, so the force on people is smaller.

Example

A truck and a car collide. Which feels a bigger force?

Third law: equal forces.

Answer: Neither; the forces are equal.

Example

A swimmer pushes water back. What pushes the swimmer forward?

Reaction force.

Answer: the water

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the bigger object pushes harder.
  • Thinking action and reaction cancel out. They act on different objects.
  • Thinking the reaction happens after the action.

faq.a: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on the other object.

faq.q: In a collision, which object feels the bigger force?
faq.a: Neither. Both feel forces of the same size, but the object with less mass changes its speed more.

faq.q: How do helmets and airbags use physics?
faq.a: They make a collision last longer, which spreads out the force and reduces the force on a person.

items.q: When you push on a wall, what does the wall do?
c: Nothing.
It pulls you toward it.
It pushes back harder.
It pushes back on you with the same size force.
items.e: That is why you can feel the wall.

items.q: Grace writes an action force: “A bird's wings push air down.” What is the reaction force?
c: The ground pushes the runner forward.
The gas pushes the rocket upward.
The nail pushes back on the hammer with an equal force.
The air pushes the wings up.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: Mia writes an action force: “A skater pushes against a wall.” What is the reaction force?
c: The boat is pushed backward away from the dock.
The wall pushes the skater away.
The road pushes the car forward.
The ground pushes the runner forward.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: What does Newton's third law say?
c: Heavier objects push harder.
Objects at rest stay at rest.
For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.
Forces only act on one object.
items.e: Forces always come in pairs.

items.q: Do action and reaction forces happen at the same time?
c: Only in collisions.
Yes, at exactly the same time.
No, the reaction comes later.
Only for heavy objects.
items.e: They are simultaneous.

The boat is pushed backward away from the dock.
The nail pushes back on the hammer with an equal force.
The road pushes the car forward.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: Ruby writes an action force: “A person steps off a small boat onto a dock.” What is the reaction force?
c: The ground pushes the runner forward.
The wall pushes the skater away.
The cannonball pushes the cannon backward (recoil).
The boat is pushed backward away from the dock.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: Why should two carts of different mass be tested several times in a collision experiment?
c: to waste time
to get reliable results
to change Newton's law
to make the carts heavier
items.e: Repeat trials.

items.q: Lily notices: “Cars have crumple zones at the front.” How does this design protect people or objects?
c: It removes Newton's third law.
The front crumples slowly, which lengthens the collision time and lowers the force on passengers.
It makes the reaction force bigger.
It makes the object heavier so nothing moves.
items.e: Spreading a collision over more time reduces the force.

In Eli's test, cart B has 3 times the mass of cart A. Cart A rolls away at 6 m/s. About how fast does cart B roll the other way?

items.e: Equal forces: 3 times the mass gives 1/3 the speed: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

items.q: A student says the heavier cart pushed harder in the collision. How would you correct this?
c: Neither cart pushed.
Both carts pushed with equal force; the lighter cart changed speed more.
The lighter cart pushed harder.
The student is right.
items.e: Newton's third law.

items.q: Nora asks: when an adult and a child collide, which one feels the bigger force?
c: Both feel forces of the same size.
Neither feels a force.
A child feels a bigger force.
An adult feels a bigger force.
items.e: Newton's third law: the forces are equal and opposite.

items.q: Leo designs a cart bumper and tests it with a force sensor. Which result shows the best design?
c: the largest peak force
the fastest bounce
the loudest crash
the smallest peak force when the cart hits the wall
items.e: Lower force means more protection.
